  • Find: The correct preposition among the choices.

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | GA Q3
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
The sum of the following infinite series is:
\( \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dfrac{1}{4!} + \dfrac{1}{5!} + \cdots \)
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Domain: Quantitative
  • Bloom’s Level: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Maclaurin / Taylor series expansion of the exponential function.
  • Given: The infinite series \( \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dfrac{1}{4!} + \dfrac{1}{5!} + \dots \).
  • Find: The exact sum of the series.

Solution (Concept + Execution)

  • Rule: The Maclaurin series expansion for \( e^x \) is defined universally as:
    \[e^x = 1 + \dfrac{x}{1!} + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \dots \]
  • Execution: Substitute \( x = 1 \) into the series:
    \[e^1 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dots \]
    The given series lacks the leading integer \( 1 \). Let \( S \) represent the given infinite series.
    \[e = 1 + S \implies S = e - 1 \]

Final Answer

Answer: (C) \( e - 1 \)
(Derived directly by setting \( x=1 \) in the exponential Maclaurin series and isolating the fractional terms.)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | GA Q4
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: A thin wire is used to construct all the edges of a cube of 1 m side by bending, cutting and soldering the wire. If the wire is 12 m long, what is the minimum number of cuts required to construct the wire frame to form the cube?
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Logic

Problem Analysis

  • Domain: Analytical / Spatial
  • Bloom’s Level: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Graph Theory (Eulerian paths), odd-degree vertices.
  • Given: A single \( 12\text{ m} \) long wire used to construct a cube with \( 1\text{ m} \) edges by bending, cutting, and soldering.
  • Find: The absolute minimum number of cuts required.

Solution (Concept + Execution)

  • Rule: A cube can be modeled as a spatial graph consisting of \( 12 \) edges and \( 8 \) vertices. At every vertex, exactly \( 3 \) edges meet.
  • Analysis: Since all \( 8 \) vertices have an odd degree (\( 3 \)), it is topologically impossible to trace the entire frame in one continuous Eulerian path without retracing edges.
    The minimum number of distinct, continuous paths required to draw a graph without retracing is \( \dfrac{\text{Number of odd vertices}}{2} \).
    \[\text{Required paths} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4 \text{ pieces} \]
  • To divide a single continuous \( 12\text{ m} \) wire into exactly \( 4 \) segments, one must make:
    \[\text{Cuts} = \text{Pieces} - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 \]
  • These \( 4 \) separate continuous pieces can then be bent appropriately and soldered to form the full cube.

Final Answer

Answer: (A) \( 3 \)
(A cube requires \( 4 \) continuous topological paths due to its \( 8 \) odd-degree vertices; yielding \( 4 \) pieces from one wire demands precisely \( 3 \) cuts.)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | GA Q7
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: Rohit goes to a restaurant for lunch at about 1 PM. When he enters the restaurant, he notices that the hour and minute hands on the wall clock are exactly coinciding. After about an hour, when he leaves the restaurant, he notices that the clock hands are again exactly coinciding. How much time (in minutes) did Rohit spend at the restaurant?
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Numerical Relations and Reasoning

Problem Analysis

  • Domain: Quantitative / Analytical
  • Bloom’s Level: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Relative speed and periodic motion of clock hands.
  • Given: An individual observes the hour and minute hands exactly coinciding at \( \approx 1\text{ PM} \), and they coincide again perfectly when he leaves.
  • Find: The duration spent, mathematically representing the exact time interval between two consecutive clock hand coincidences.

Solution (Concept + Execution)

  • Rule: In a standard 12-hour clock, the minute hand travels at \( 360^\circ / 60\text{ min} = 6^\circ/\text{min} \). The hour hand travels at \( 360^\circ / 720\text{ min} = 0.5^\circ/\text{min} \).
  • The relative angular speed between the hands is \( 6^\circ - 0.5^\circ = 5.5^\circ/\text{min} \).
  • For the minute hand to lap the hour hand and coincide again, it must cover a relative angular distance of precisely \( 360^\circ \).
  • Calculation:
    \[\text{Time} = \dfrac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Relative Speed}} = \dfrac{360}{5.5} = \dfrac{720}{11} \text{ minutes} \]
  • Converting the improper fraction to a mixed number:
    \[\dfrac{720}{11} = 65 \dfrac{5}{11} \text{ minutes} \]

Final Answer

Answer: (C) \( 65 \dfrac{5}{11} \) minutes
(Standard clock mechanics dictate that hands coincide exactly every \( 720/11 \) minutes.)

  • Find: The valid spatial intersection of these codes.

Solution (Concept + Execution)

  • Rule: In standard subtractive color mixing (CMYK), overlapping primary pigments produces secondary colors:
    \( \text{Cyan (Cy)} \cap \text{Yellow (Y)} = \text{Green (G)} \)
    \( \text{Yellow (Y)} \cap \text{Magenta (M)} = \text{Red (R)} \)
    \( \text{Cyan (Cy)} \cap \text{Magenta (M)} = \text{Blue (Bl)} \)
    \( \text{Cyan (Cy)} \cap \text{Magenta (M)} \cap \text{Yellow (Y)} = \text{Black (K)} \)
  • Execution: The correct diagram must represent C, M, and Y as the three primary sets (main circles). The pairwise intersections must contain G, R, and Bl respectively. The three-way central intersection must contain K. Option (A) strictly maps this set-theoretic relationship without contradictions.

Answer: (A)
(It properly reflects the geometric intersections of the subtractive color model where primary sets overlap to form secondary colors and a black center.)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | GA Q9
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: A circle with center at \((x, y) = (0.5, 0)\) and radius \(= 0.5\) intersects with another circle with center at \((x, y) = (1, 1)\) and radius \(= 1\) at two points. One of the points of intersection \((x, y)\) is:
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Domain: Quantitative
  • Bloom’s Level: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Coordinate geometry (Intersection of circles).
  • Given: Circle 1: Center \( (0.5, 0) \), Radius \( 0.5 \)
    Circle 2: Center \( (1, 1) \), Radius \( 1 \)
  • Find: A common intersection point \( (x, y) \).

Solution (Concept + Execution)

  • Step 1: Formulate the equations of the circles.
    \( C_1: (x - 0.5)^2 + y^2 = 0.5^2 \implies x^2 - x + 0.25 + y^2 = 0.25 \implies x^2 + y^2 - x = 0 \)
    \( C_2: (x - 1)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 1^2 \implies x^2 - 2x + 1 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = 1 \implies x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 2y + 1 = 0 \)
  • Step 2: Subtract \( C_1 \) from \( C_2 \) to find the common radical axis (a linear relation between coordinates).
    \( (x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 2y + 1) - (x^2 + y^2 - x) = 0 \)
    \( -x - 2y + 1 = 0 \implies x = 1 - 2y \)
  • Step 3: Substitute \( x \) back into \( C_1 \).
    \( (1 - 2y)^2 + y^2 - (1 - 2y) = 0 \)
    \( 1 - 4y + 4y^2 + y^2 - 1 + 2y = 0 \implies 5y^2 - 2y = 0 \implies y(5y - 2) = 0 \)
  • Step 4: Solve for the coordinate pairs.
    If \( y = 0 \), \( x = 1 - 2(0) = 1 \). Intersection 1: \( (1, 0) \)
    If \( y = 0.4 \), \( x = 1 - 2(0.4) = 0.2 \). Intersection 2: \( (0.2, 0.4) \)
  • Comparing with choices, \( (0.2, 0.4) \) is an available option.

Final Answer

Answer: (B) \( (0.2, 0.4) \)
(Solving the circle equations simultaneously yields the discrete coordinate intersections \( (1,0) \) and \( (0.2,0.4) \).)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Suppose \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of matrix \(A\) and \(x\) is the corresponding eigenvector. Let \(x\) also be an eigenvector of the matrix \(B = A - 2I\), where \(I\) is the identity matrix. Then, the eigenvalue of \(B\) corresponding to the eigenvector \(x\) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra / Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: 3. Application
  • Given Data: Matrix \(A\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with the corresponding eigenvector \(x\). Matrix \(B = A - 2I\), where \(I\) is the identity matrix.
  • Aim: Find the eigenvalue of matrix \(B\) corresponding to the eigenvector \(x\).

3. Core Concepts:

Eigenvalue Equation: For a square matrix \(A\), an eigenvector \(x\) and its corresponding eigenvalue \(\lambda\) satisfy the equation: \(Ax = \lambda x\).

Matrix Polynomials: If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\), then for any scalar \(k\), the matrix \((A - kI)\) will have an eigenvalue of \((\lambda - k)\) corresponding to the exact same eigenvector \(x\).

4. Solution Method:

  • We start with the fundamental eigenvalue equation for matrix \(B\).
  • Substitute \(B = A - 2I\) and apply matrix distribution.
  • Substitute \(Ax\) with \(\lambda x\) and factor out the eigenvector \(x\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Write the eigenvalue equation for \(B\):
    \[Bx = (A - 2I)x \]
  2. Distribute the vector \(x\) inside the parenthesis:
    \[Bx = Ax - 2Ix \]
  3. Since \(I\) is the identity matrix, \(Ix = x\). Also, from the given data, \(Ax = \lambda x\). Substitute these into the equation:
    \[Bx = \lambda x - 2x \]
  4. Factor out the common vector \(x\):
    \[Bx = (\lambda - 2)x \]
  5. By definition, since \(Bx = \text{scalar} \cdot x\), the scalar \((\lambda - 2)\) is the eigenvalue of matrix \(B\) corresponding to the eigenvector \(x\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\lambda - 2\) | Option(s): D

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(b = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3 \end{bmatrix}\). For \(Ax = b\) to be solvable, which one of the following options is the correct condition on \(b_1, b_2\), and \(b_3\):
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra / System of Linear Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: 4. Analysis & Synthesis
  • Given Data: Coefficient matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\)
    Constant vector \(b = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3 \end{bmatrix}\)
  • Aim: Determine the algebraic condition on \(b_1, b_2, \text{ and } b_3\) for the system \(Ax = b\) to be consistent (solvable).

3. Core Concepts:

Rouché-Capelli Theorem: A system of linear equations \(Ax = b\) is solvable (consistent) if and only if the rank of the coefficient matrix \(A\) is equal to the rank of the augmented matrix \([A|b]\).

Row Echelon Form: Applying elementary row operations to reduce the augmented matrix helps identify conditions required to maintain equal ranks.

4. Solution Method:

  • Construct the augmented matrix \([A|b]\).
  • Perform Gaussian elimination (elementary row operations) to convert matrix \(A\) into an upper triangular form.
  • Since \(A\) has dimensions \(3 \times 2\), its maximum rank is 2. The 3rd row of the reduced matrix \(A\) will become strictly zeros.
  • For the system to be solvable, the corresponding 3rd row entry in the constant vector column must also equate to zero.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Form the augmented matrix:
    \[ [A|b] = \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 1 & b_1 \\ 1 & 3 & b_2 \\ -2 & -3 & b_3 \end{array}\right] \]
  2. Eliminate the entries below the pivot in the first column:
    \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\)
    \(R_3 \to R_3 + 2R_1\)
    \[ [A|b] = \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 1 & b_1 \\ 0 & 2 & b_2 - b_1 \\ 0 & -1 & b_3 + 2b_1 \end{array}\right] \]
  3. Eliminate the entry below the pivot in the second column to create a row of zeros in the coefficient side:
    \(R_3 \to 2R_3 + R_2\)
    \(R_3 \text{ transformation:} \quad 2(0) + 0 = 0 \quad | \quad 2(-1) + 2 = 0 \quad | \quad 2(b_3 + 2b_1) + (b_2 - b_1)\)
    \[ [A|b] = \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 1 & b_1 \\ 0 & 2 & b_2 - b_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4b_1 + 2b_3 + b_2 - b_1 \end{array}\right] \]
  4. Simplify the expression in the \(3^{rd}\) row, constant column:
    \[3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 \]
  5. For the system to be solvable, rank(\(A\)) = rank(\([A|b]\)), thus the term corresponding to the zero-row must be zero:
    \[3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0\) | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Which one of the following options is the correct Fourier series of the periodic function \(f(x)\) described below:

\( f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } -2 < x < -1 \\ 2k & \text{if } -1 < x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{if } 1 < x < 2 \end{cases} \);  period = 4
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus / Fourier Series

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: 3. Application
  • Given Data: \(f(x) = 0\) for \(-2 < x < -1\)
    \(f(x) = 2k\) for \(-1 < x < 1\)
    \(f(x) = 0\) for \(1 < x < 2\)
    Period \(T = 4\)
  • Aim: Identify the correct Fourier series expansion for the periodic function \(f(x)\).

3. Core Concepts:

Fourier Series Representation: \(f(x) = \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right) + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\)

Half-Period (\(L\)): \(T = 2L \implies L = 2\).

Even/Odd Function Check: \(f(x)\) is symmetrical about the y-axis, hence it is an even function. For even functions, all sine terms vanish (\(b_n = 0\)).

4. Solution Method:

  • Verify \(b_n = 0\) to instantly eliminate options containing sine terms.
  • Calculate the DC component / constant term \(a_0 / 2\).
  • Calculate the general cosine coefficient \(a_n\) and expand for \(n = 1, 2, 3...\) to match the correct option.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine \(a_0\):
    \[a_0 = \dfrac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) dx = \dfrac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} f(x) dx \]
    \[ a_0 = \dfrac{2}{2} \int_{0}^{1} 2k \, dx + \int_{1}^{2} 0 \, dx = [2kx]_0^1 = 2k \]
    Therefore, the constant term in the series \(\dfrac{a_0}{2} = \dfrac{2k}{2} = k\). (This eliminates Option A).
  2. Determine \(a_n\):
    \[a_n = \dfrac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} f(x) \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right) dx = \dfrac{2}{2} \int_{0}^{1} 2k \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right) dx \]
    \[ a_n = 2k \left[\dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)}{\dfrac{n\pi}{2}} \right]_0^1 = \dfrac{4k}{n\pi} \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}\right) \]
  3. Evaluate \(a_n\) for different values of \(n\):
    For \(n=1\): \(a_1 = \dfrac{4k}{\pi} \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{4k}{\pi}\)
    For \(n=2\): \(a_2 = \dfrac{4k}{2\pi} \sin(\pi) = 0\)
    For \(n=3\): \(a_3 = \dfrac{4k}{3\pi} \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}\)
    For \(n=4\): \(a_4 = 0\)
    For \(n=5\): \(a_5 = \dfrac{4k}{5\pi} \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{4k}{5\pi}\)
  4. Construct the final Fourier series:
    \[f(x) = k + \dfrac{4k}{\pi} \left( \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}x\right) - \dfrac{1}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}x\right) + \dfrac{1}{5}\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2}x\right) - \dots \right) \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(f(x)=k+\dfrac{4k}{\pi}(cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}x-\dfrac{1}{3}cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}x+\dfrac{1}{5}cos\dfrac{5\pi}{2}x-+\dots)\) | Option(s): C

questions.question:
X is a random variable that can take any one of the values 0, 1, 7, 11, and 12. The probability mass function for X is
\(P(X = 0) = 0.4\); \(P(X = 1) = 0.3\); \(P(X = 7) = 0.1\);
\(P(X = 11) = 0.1\); \(P(X = 12) = 0.1\)
Then, the variance of X is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability and Statistics / Random Variables

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: 3. Application
  • Given Data: Random Variable \(X \in \{0, 1, 7, 11, 12\}\)
    PMF: \(P(X=0)=0.4\); \(P(X=1)=0.3\); \(P(X=7)=0.1\); \(P(X=11)=0.1\); \(P(X=12)=0.1\)
  • Aim: Calculate the variance of \(X\).

3. Core Concepts:

Expected Value (Mean): \(E[X] = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i)\)

Expected Value of Squares: \(E[X^2] = \sum x_i^2 \cdot P(x_i)\)

Variance Formula: \(\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2\)

4. Solution Method:

  • Verify that the sum of probabilities is 1.0 (Sanity check: \(0.4+0.3+0.1+0.1+0.1 = 1.0\), OK).
  • Compute the expected value \(E[X]\).

questions.question: The results of a consolidated drained triaxial test on a normally consolidated clay are shown in the figure. The angle of internal friction is
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength of Soils

Taxonomy and Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: 3. Application
  • Given Data:
    Minor principal stress (cell pressure), \( \sigma_3 = 50 \text{ kPa} \)
    Major principal stress at failure, \( \sigma_1 = 100 \text{ kPa} \)
    Soil Type: Normally consolidated (NC) clay
  • Aim: Determine the angle of internal friction (\(\phi\)) of the soil sample.

Core Concepts

Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion: Defines the shear strength of soil in terms of effective stresses.

Normally Consolidated (NC) Clay: For an NC clay subjected to a consolidated drained (CD) test, the effective cohesion intercept is zero (\(c' = 0 \text{ kPa}\)). The strength envelope passes through the origin.

Principal Stress Relationship: The general relationship between major and minor principal stresses at failure is given by:
\[\sigma_1 = \sigma_3 \tan^2\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) + 2c \tan\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) \]
For a cohesionless soil or NC clay (\(c=0\)), this simplifies directly to the geometric property of the Mohr circle touching the failure envelope:
\[\sin \phi = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{\sigma_1 + \sigma_3} \]

Solution Method

  • Identify the principal stresses from the provided Mohr circle diagram.
  • Apply the simplified principal stress relationship for \(c=0\) soils to solve for \(\sin \phi\).
  • Take the inverse sine to find the angle \(\phi\).

Common Pitfall: Assuming a non-zero cohesion for a normally consolidated clay. Always remember CD tests on true NC clays yield \(c' = 0\).

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Extract values from diagram: The Mohr circle intersects the normal stress (\(\sigma\)) axis at \(50 \text{ kPa}\) and \(100 \text{ kPa}\). Thus:
    \(\sigma_3 = 50 \text{ kPa}\)
    \(\sigma_1 = 100 \text{ kPa}\)
  2. Establish cohesion: Since the soil is a normally consolidated clay, effective cohesion \(c = 0 \text{ kPa}\).
  3. Apply standard relationship:
    \[\sin \phi = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{\sigma_1 + \sigma_3} \]
  4. Substitute the stress values:
    \[\sin \phi = \dfrac{100 \text{ kPa} - 50 \text{ kPa}}{100 \text{ kPa} + 50 \text{ kPa}} \]
    \[\sin \phi = \dfrac{50}{150} \]
    \[\sin \phi = \dfrac{1}{3} \]
  5. Solve for \(\phi\):
    \[\phi = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \]

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity Check: The calculated angle evaluates to approximately \(19.47^\circ\). This is a highly realistic effective friction angle for a normally consolidated clay deposit. \(\sin \phi \le 1\) is satisfied.

Final Answer

Final Answer: \(\sin^{-1}(1/3)\) | Option(s): B

  3. Read the position relative to the A-line (above or below).

A hydrocarbon (\( C_nH_m \)) is burnt in air (\( O_2 + 3.78N_2 \)). The stoichiometric fuel to air mass ratio for this process is
Note: Atomic Weight: C(12), H(1)
      Effective Molecular Weight: Air(28.8)
      Ignore any conversion of \( N_2 \) in air to the oxides of nitrogen (\( NO_x \))
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution / Combustion Stoichiometry

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Hydrocarbon formula: \(C_nH_m\)
    Oxidant: Air (\(O_2 + 3.78N_2\))
    Atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1
    Effective molecular weight of air = 28.8
  • Aim: Find the stoichiometric fuel to air mass ratio.

Core Concepts:

Stoichiometry: Balance the combustion equation assuming complete oxidation of Carbon to \(CO_2\) and Hydrogen to \(H_2O\).

Air Composition: For every 1 mole of \(O_2\) required, \((1 + 3.78) = 4.78\) moles of air are drawn.

Solution:

  1. Balanced combustion equation:
    \[C_nH_m + \left(n + \dfrac{m}{4}\right)O_2 \rightarrow nCO_2 + \dfrac{m}{2}H_2O \]
  2. Moles of \(O_2\) required per mole of fuel:
    \[n + \dfrac{m}{4} = \dfrac{4n+m}{4} \]
  3. Total moles of air required:
    \(4.78\) moles of air per mole of \(O_2\), so total air moles \(= 4.78 \times \dfrac{4n+m}{4}\)
  4. Mass of 1 mole of fuel: \((12n + m)\)
  5. Mass of required air:
    \[4.78 \times \dfrac{4n+m}{4} \times 28.8 = 34.416(4n+m) \]
  6. Fuel to Air Mass Ratio:
    \[\dfrac{12n+m}{34.416(4n+m)} = \dfrac{1}{34.416} \times \dfrac{12n+m}{4n+m} \approx 0.02905 \times \dfrac{12n+m}{4n+m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(0.0291\,\dfrac{(12n+m)}{(4n+m)}\) | Option: D

Problem Analysis

  • Aim: Convert the given quadrantal bearing to whole circle bearing (WCB).

Core Concepts

Theory: A quadrantal bearing is measured from the nearer North/South meridian toward East/West, limited to \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\). A whole circle bearing is measured clockwise from North, ranging \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\).

Formulas (QB \(\to\) WCB):
Let \(\theta\) be the acute angle in the quadrantal bearing.

  • NE quadrant (N\(\theta\)E): \(\text{WCB} = \theta\)
  • SE quadrant (S\(\theta\)E): \(\text{WCB} = 180^\circ - \theta\)
  • SW quadrant (S\(\theta\)W): \(\text{WCB} = 180^\circ + \theta\)
  • NW quadrant (N\(\theta\)W): \(\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - \theta\)

Standard assumptions: Bearings are referenced to North; WCB is measured clockwise.

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: Identify the quadrant from the QB notation (N/S first, then E/W) \(\rightarrow\) choose the corresponding conversion formula \(\rightarrow\) compute WCB.
  • Alternative: Visualize the azimuth clockwise from North; for N\(\theta\)W, rotate \(\theta\) anticlockwise from North, hence clockwise bearing is \(360^\circ-\theta\).
  • Common pitfalls to avoid: (i) Using \(180^\circ \pm \theta\) for NW cases, (ii) forgetting that WCB is clockwise from North.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Identify quadrant: \(\text{N}30^\circ\text{W}\) lies in the NW quadrant (from North towards West) with \(\theta = 30^\circ\).
  2. Apply NW conversion:
    \[\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - \theta \]
  3. Substitute and compute:
    \[\text{WCB} = 360^\circ - 30^\circ = 330^\circ \]

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: NW bearings must yield WCB between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\). The computed \(330^\circ\) satisfies this, so the result is physically consistent.

Final Answer

Final Answer: \(330^\circ\) | Option(s): D

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Partial Differential Equations (Order, Linearity, Homogeneity)

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Four differential equations involving \(u\) and its partial derivatives (options A–D), with constant \(c\) and independent variables \(x,y,z,t\).
  • Aim: Identify which equation(s) are second-order, linear, and homogeneous partial differential equations.

Core Concepts

Theory:

  • Order: The highest order of partial derivative present in the equation.
  • Linearity: A PDE is linear if \(u\) and all its derivatives appear to the first power and are not multiplied together or inside nonlinear functions. Coefficients may depend on independent variables, but not on \(u\).
  • Homogeneity: A linear PDE is homogeneous if it can be written as \(L(u)=0\), i.e., there is no term independent of \(u\) (no forcing/source term like \(xy\), constants, etc.).

Canonical linear homogeneous form:
\[L(u) = 0 \]
where \(L\) is a linear differential operator (e.g., Laplacian, wave operator).

Standard assumptions: The classification is based purely on the mathematical structure (order, linearity, and presence/absence of forcing term), not on boundary/initial conditions.

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: For each option: (i) determine the highest derivative order \( ightarrow\) (ii) test linearity (no powers/products of derivatives) \( ightarrow\) (iii) test homogeneity (no standalone forcing term).
  • Alternatives: Rewrite each equation in operator form \(L(u)=f\). If \(f=0\), it is homogeneous; if \(f eq 0\), non-homogeneous.
  • Common pitfalls to avoid: (i) Calling an equation “homogeneous” just because \(u\) terms look similar on both sides; (ii) overlooking nonlinearities like \((u_{tt})^2\); (iii) confusing first-order PDE with second-order PDE.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Option (A):
    \(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2\left(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} ight) + xy\)
    Order: second (contains \(u_{tt}, u_{xx}, u_{yy}\)).
    Linearity: linear in \(u\) and its derivatives.
    Homogeneity test: presence of forcing term \(xy\) (independent of \(u\)) implies \(L(u)=xy eq 0\). Hence non-homogeneous. Reject.
  2. Option (B):
    \(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}+\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}+\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2}=0\)
    Order: second (highest derivative is second).
    Linearity: each derivative appears to the first power; no products/nonlinear functions. So linear.
    Homogeneity: right-hand side is zero, i.e., \(L(u)=0\). So homogeneous. Accept.
  3. Option (C):
    \(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = c\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}\)
    Order: first (only first derivatives). Therefore it is not second-order. Reject.
  4. Option (D):
    \(\left(\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} ight)^2 = c^2\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}\)
    Order: second (contains second derivatives).
    Linearity test: term \(\left(u_{tt} ight)^2\) is a square of a derivative, hence the equation is nonlinear. Reject.
  5. Conclusion: Only option (B) satisfies all three conditions: second-order, linear, homogeneous.

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: Option (B) is the classic 3D Laplace equation \( abla^2 u=0\), which is universally recognized as second-order, linear, homogeneous. All rejections are consistent with standard definitions (forcing term in A, order mismatch in C, nonlinearity in D).

Final Answer

Final Answer: Option(s): B

questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Rigid Frame under Joint Couples (Symmetry & Member Actions)

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Joint couples: \(M_B = 100\ \text{kN\m}\), \(M_G = 100\ \text{kN\m}\) (applied at joints B and G).
    Geometry (from figure): storey height \(h = 6\ \text{m}\); bay lengths \(L_1 = 8\ \text{m}\), \(L_2 = 8\ \text{m}\).
    Flexural rigidities are piecewise (shown as \(2EI\), \(4EI\), etc.).
    Modeling statement: “Considering only effects of flexural deformations” \(\Rightarrow\) axial deformations are neglected (members assumed axially very stiff), bending governs compatibility.
  • Aim: Decide which statements about member CD and joint C are true.

Core Concepts

1) Symmetry in frames: If the geometry and stiffness distribution are symmetric about a vertical axis and the loading is also symmetric, the deflected shape is symmetric. On the axis of symmetry, the rotation (slope) is zero (a “mirror” condition).

2) Member with no intermediate transverse load: For a prismatic member with no distributed/point load along its length, the bending moment varies linearly between end moments. Hence the shear force is constant and given by
\[V = \dfrac{M_{\text{right}} - M_{\text{left}}}{L} \]
Therefore, shear \(V=0\) iff end moments are equal: \(M_{\text{right}} = M_{\text{left}}\).

3) Slope-deflection (conceptual form): For a member \(ij\) (no span load), end moments depend on end rotations \(\theta_i,\theta_j\) and chord rotation \(\psi\) (from joint translation):
\[M_{ij} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\left(2\theta_i + \theta_j - 3\psi\right),\quad M_{ji} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\left(2\theta_j + \theta_i - 3\psi\right) \]
If \(\theta_i = \theta_j\) and \(\psi=0\), then \(M_{ij}=M_{ji}\) \(\Rightarrow\) shear in that member is zero.

4) Important modeling note (flexure-only): “Neglect axial deformations” does not imply axial force is zero. It implies axial strain energy is neglected (axial rigidity effectively infinite), so axial forces may develop to satisfy equilibrium/compatibility without producing significant axial deformation.

Standard assumptions: Small deflections, linear elastic behavior, plane sections remain plane, rigid joints.

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: (i) Recognize symmetry of frame and loading, (ii) impose symmetry boundary condition at joint C, (iii) use no-span-load relation to infer shear in CD, (iv) use moment-sharing argument at joint C to assess statement about moment in BC.
  • Alternative view: Analyze only half the frame by cutting at the symmetry axis and applying symmetry constraints (rotation zero at the cut line).
  • Common pitfalls to avoid:
    (i) Concluding “axial force = 0” just because axial deformations are neglected.
    (ii) Confusing the Bernoulli-type “no shear implies no bending” (false): a member can carry constant bending moment with zero shear.
    (iii) Forgetting that joint moments are distributed among all connecting members based on relative stiffness.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Identify structural symmetry:
    The frame geometry and member stiffness pattern are symmetric about the vertical line passing through joints \(D\)–\(C\). The applied couples at joints \(B\) and \(G\) have equal magnitudes (\(100\ \text{kN\m}\)) and are placed symmetrically with respect to the same axis. Hence the loading is symmetric.
  2. Apply symmetry boundary condition at joint C:
    For symmetric loading on a symmetric structure, the deflected shape is symmetric. Therefore, the axis of symmetry has zero slope (mirror condition). Since joint \(C\) lies on the symmetry axis, the rotation at joint C is zero:
    \[\theta_C = 0 \]
    This directly makes statement (C) true.
  3. Relate shear in member CD to end moments:
    Member \(CD\) has no intermediate transverse loading along its length (only joint actions). Therefore shear in \(CD\) is constant and given by
    \[V_{CD} = \dfrac{M_{DC} - M_{CD}}{L_{CD}} \]
    where \(L_{CD}=6\ \text{m}\).
  4. Use symmetry to establish equal end moments in CD:
    Because the member \(CD\) lies on the symmetry axis, the chord rotation due to sidesway across the symmetry axis is zero: \(\psi_{CD}=0\). Also, symmetry implies identical rotational restraint at joints \(C\) and \(D\) on the axis, giving \(\theta_C=\theta_D\) (and from Step 2, \(\theta_C=0\Rightarrow\theta_D=0\)). Substituting \(\theta_C=\theta_D\) and \(\psi_{CD}=0\) into the slope-deflection expressions yields
    \[M_{CD} = M_{DC} \]
    Hence,
    \[V_{CD} = \dfrac{M_{DC} - M_{CD}}{6} = 0\ \text{kN} \]
    So statement (B) is true.
  5. Check statement (A) about axial force in CD:
    Even though axial deformations are neglected, axial forces may develop in rigid frames to enforce joint translation compatibility (especially when couples induce joint shears and frame-action). Therefore there is no basis to conclude \(N_{CD}=0\). Hence statement (A) is not necessarily true (treated as false).
  6. Assess statement (D) (moment at end C of BC):
    At joint \(C\), member \(BC\) is not the only member providing rotational stiffness; at least one other member (notably \(CD\), and depending on connectivity also \(CG\)) shares the joint moment. In moment distribution terms, the distribution factor for member \(BC\) at joint \(C\) is \[DF_{BC} = \dfrac{k_{BC}}{\sum k}\ ,\quad 0 \ < DF_{BC} \ < 0.5 \]
    because \(\sum k\) includes stiffness contributions from other connected members, making the denominator larger than \(k_{BC}+k_{BC}\). Thus \(BC\) cannot attract more than half of the joint unbalanced moment; therefore the end moment at \(C\) in member \(BC\) cannot exceed \(50 \text{kN\,m}\) in magnitude for a \(100 \text{kN\,m}\) scale of couple-induced joint action. Hence statement (D) is false.

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: (i) Zero rotation at the symmetry axis is a standard, physically consistent boundary condition under symmetric loading. (ii) Zero shear in a member with equal end moments and no span load is consistent with \(V=\Delta M/L\). (iii) Moment at a joint must be shared by connected members based on stiffness, so “more than 50 kN·m” for one member is unlikely when multiple members contribute.

Final Answer

Final Answer: Statements (B) and (C) are true | Option(s): B, C

questions.question: For the Bernoulli’s equation to be applicable in a fluid flow situation, which of the following conditions is/are to be satisfied:
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Applicability Conditions of Bernoulli’s Equation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    A set of proposed conditions for applying Bernoulli’s equation in a fluid-flow situation:
    (A) frictionless, (B) incompressible, (C) steady, (D) rotational.
  • Aim: Identify the condition(s) that must be satisfied for Bernoulli’s equation to be applicable.

Core Concepts

1) Origin of Bernoulli’s equation: It is obtained by integrating Euler’s equation along a streamline for an inviscid (frictionless) flow. For the commonly used engineering form between two points, it is written as\[\dfrac{p}{\gamma} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{constant} \]

2) Required conditions (engineering form):

  • Frictionless (inviscid): Viscous dissipation must be negligible; otherwise head loss terms must be added.
  • Incompressible: Density \( ho\) is constant (valid for liquids and low-speed gas flows where density change is negligible).
  • Steady: Flow properties do not change with time at a fixed point, so the energy balance remains time-invariant.

3) Rotational vs irrotational:
For a rotational flow, Bernoulli’s constant can differ from one streamline to another; the equation is still valid along a given streamline (subject to inviscid, incompressible, steady conditions). For the strongest/general statement “applicable in a flow situation” (i.e., usable between arbitrary points without specifying same streamline), the flow should be irrotational, not rotational. Therefore, “flow should be rotational” is not a required condition and is generally the opposite of the added requirement for global applicability.

Standard assumptions: No shaft work addition/removal (no pumps/turbines between points) and no heat transfer effects in the mechanical energy form (typical GATE Bernoulli context).

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: (i) Recall derivation assumptions of Bernoulli from Euler equation, (ii) list mandatory assumptions, (iii) evaluate each option against these assumptions.
  • Alternative: Compare with extended energy equation: if friction exists, add head loss \(h_f\); if unsteady or compressible, additional terms/relations are needed.
  • Common pitfalls to avoid:
    (i) Thinking “rotational” is required; actually “irrotational” is the extra condition for same constant across streamlines.
    (ii) Forgetting that inviscid is essential for the simple Bernoulli form without head loss.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Check option (A): frictionless
    Bernoulli’s equation in its basic form assumes negligible viscosity (no frictional head loss). Hence (A) is required.
  2. Check option (B): incompressible
    The standard Bernoulli form \(p/\gamma + V^2/(2g) + z\) assumes constant density (incompressible). Hence (B) is required.
  3. Check option (C): steady
    Classical Bernoulli derivation assumes steady flow so that the energy per unit weight is time-invariant along the streamline. Hence (C) is required.
  4. Check option (D): rotational
    Rotational flow is not a requirement. In fact, to apply Bernoulli between any two points irrespective of streamline, the flow should be irrotational. Therefore “flow should be rotational” is not a condition to be satisfied. Hence (D) is not selected.

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: The selected conditions match the standard GATE/undergraduate statement for Bernoulli applicability (inviscid, incompressible, steady). Excluding (D) is consistent because rotationality restricts Bernoulli to streamline-wise use rather than being a required prerequisite.

Final Answer

Final Answer: Conditions (A), (B), and (C) must be satisfied | Option(s): A, B, C

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Sedimentation / Stokes' Law

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) = 45 m³/m²/d
    Specific gravity of inorganic particles \(G_i\) = 2.65
    Specific gravity of organic particles \(G_o\) = 1.20
    Acceleration due to gravity \(g\) = 9.81 m/s²
    Kinematic viscosity \( u\) = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s
  • Aim: Find minimum diameters of spherical inorganic and organic particles that will be completely removed (100% removal) in the rectangular sedimentation tank.

Core Concepts:

In an ideal rectangular sedimentation tank, the surface overflow rate SOR (= Q/A) equals the critical settling velocity \(V_o\). Any discrete spherical particle whose terminal settling velocity \(V_s \ge V_o\) is removed completely irrespective of its entry height (Type-I discrete settling).

Stokes' Law (valid when Reynolds number Re < 0.5):

\[V_s = \dfrac{g(G-1)d^2}{18 u} \]

where \(V_s\) = terminal settling velocity (m/s), \(G\) = specific gravity of particle, \(d\) = particle diameter (m), \( u\) = kinematic viscosity (m²/s).

Rearranged for minimum diameter (set \(V_s = ext{SOR} = V_o\)):

\[d = \sqrt{\dfrac{18 u V_o}{g(G-1)}} \]

Unit discipline (critical): SOR must be converted from m³/m²/d → m/s before substitution.

Common pitfalls to avoid:

  • Forgetting to convert SOR from per-day to per-second.
  • Using dynamic viscosity \(\mu\) instead of kinematic \( u\).
  • Taking \(G\) instead of \((G-1)\).

Solution:

  1. Convert SOR to critical settling velocity \(V_o\) in m/s:
    SOR = 45 m³/m²/d = 45 m/d
    1 d = 24 × 3600 = 86,400 s
    \[V_o = \dfrac{45}{86400} = 5.20833 imes 10^{-4} ext{ m/s} \]
  2. Inorganic particles (\(G\) = 2.65):
    \[d_i = \sqrt{\dfrac{18 imes 1 imes 10^{-6} imes 5.20833 imes 10^{-4}}{9.81 imes (2.65-1)}} \]
    Numerator: \(18 imes 10^{-6} imes 5.20833 imes 10^{-4} = 9.375 imes 10^{-9}\)
    Denominator: \(9.81 imes 1.65 = 16.1865\)
    \[d_i^2 = \dfrac{9.375 imes 10^{-9}}{16.1865} = 5.791 imes 10^{-10} \]
    \[d_i = \sqrt{5.791 imes 10^{-10}} = 2.4065 imes 10^{-5} ext{ m} = \mathbf{24.065\ \mu m \approx 24\ \mu m} \]
  3. Organic particles (\(G\) = 1.20):
    \[d_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{18 imes 1 imes 10^{-6} imes 5.20833 imes 10^{-4}}{9.81 imes (1.20-1)}} \]
    Denominator: \(9.81 imes 0.20 = 1.962\)
    \[d_o^2 = \dfrac{9.375 imes 10^{-9}}{1.962} = 4.778 imes 10^{-9} \]
    \[d_o = \sqrt{4.778 imes 10^{-9}} = 6.9127 imes 10^{-5} ext{ m} = \mathbf{69.127\ \mu m \approx 69\ \mu m} \]

The higher density difference for inorganic particles (\(\Delta G\) = 1.65 vs 0.20) allows much smaller particles to achieve the same settling velocity, explaining why \(d_i \ll d_o\).

Final Answer:

Minimum diameter of inorganic particles = 24 µm; Minimum diameter of organic particles = 69 µm | Option(s): A, B

Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment Processes / Aeration

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Comprehension
  • Given Data: Aeration employed for removal of pollutants from contaminated water. Options: Iron, Cadmium, Manganese, Zinc.
  • Aim: Identify the pollutant(s) for which aeration is used as part of the removal process (MSQ).

Core Concepts:

Aeration supplies dissolved oxygen to oxidise soluble reduced forms of metals into insoluble oxidised forms that can then be removed by sedimentation/filtration.

  • Iron: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ (forms Fe(OH)₃ precipitate) — removed by aeration.
  • Manganese: Mn²⁺ → Mn⁴⁺ (forms MnO₂ precipitate) — removed by aeration.
  • Cadmium & Zinc: Do not undergo useful oxidation by simple aeration; require chemical precipitation (lime/sulphide), coagulation, or adsorption.

Solution:

  1. Recall purpose of aeration: gas stripping (CO₂, H₂S) + oxidation of Fe & Mn.
  2. Iron: Aeration oxidises ferrous iron — classic process in groundwater treatment. ✓
  3. Manganese: Requires aeration (often with pH adjustment) to form insoluble MnO₂. ✓
  4. Cadmium & Zinc: Removed by pH elevation + precipitation or ion exchange; aeration alone is ineffective. ✗

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Iron and Manganese | Option(s): A; C

questions.question: A water resources project with an expected life of 25 years has to be designed for an acceptable risk of 5% against a design flood. The return period for the design flood (in years) is _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Flood Risk & Return Period

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Expected project life \(n\) = 25 years
    Acceptable risk \(R\) = 5% = 0.05
  • Aim: Return period (\(T\)) of the design flood (rounded off to nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

Risk \(R\) = probability that the design flood will be exceeded at least once in \(n\) years.

\[R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n \]

Standard in hydrological design of water resources projects (IS 6966 for dams, IRC guidelines for bridges).

Solution:

  1. Substitute known values:
    \[0.05 = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^{25} \]
    \[\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^{25} = 0.95 \]
  2. Take the 25th root of both sides:
    \[1 - \dfrac{1}{T} = 0.95^{1/25} \]
  3. Evaluate:
    \[0.95^{1/25} = 0.99795037 \]
  4. Solve for \(T\):
    \[\dfrac{1}{T} = 1 - 0.99795037 = 0.00204963 \]
    \[T = \dfrac{1}{0.00204963} \approx 487.89 \text{ years} \]
  5. Rounded to nearest integer = 488 years
    Note: Approximate formula for small R gives \(T \approx n/R = 500\) years; both lie in the official accepted range.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 488 | (Range 476 to 500)

questions.question:
Road A and Road B are joined by a circular horizontal curve of radius 200 m as shown in the figure. Road A and Road B are tangential to the curve at the points C and D, respectively. Had the curve not been there, straight roads A and B would have met at the point E. The distance from C to E is 92 m. The value of angle θ (in degrees) is _______________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
Note: The value of angle θ is to be calculated only from the consideration of Euclidean geometry and the data given in the problem.
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Geometric Design of Highways

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Radius of horizontal curve, \(R = 200\) m
    Tangent length (C to E), \(T = 92\) m
    Roads A and B are tangents meeting at point E.
  • Aim: Calculate the intersection/deflection angle \(\theta\) in degrees.

Core Concepts:

Circular Curve Geometry: For a simple circular curve connecting two straight tangents, the distance from the point of tangency (PC) to the point of intersection (PI) is the tangent length (\(T\)).

Tangent Length Formula:

\[T = R \tan\left(\dfrac{\Delta}{2}\right) \]

where \(\Delta\) is the deflection angle between the two tangents. The angle \(\theta\) corresponds exactly to this deflection angle \(\Delta\).

Solution:

  1. Set up the equation:
    \[92 = 200 \tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) \]
  2. Solve for the trigonometric ratio:
    \[\tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{92}{200} = 0.46 \]
  3. Calculate the half-angle:
    \[\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \arctan(0.46) \approx 24.7024° \]
  4. Calculate \(\theta\):
    \[\theta = 2 \times 24.7024° = 49.4048° \approx 49.4° \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 49.4° | Official Key Range: 48 to 51

questions.question: The value of \( \lim_{x \to \infty} (x - \sqrt{x^2 + x}) \) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus / Limits

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: The limit expression \(\lim_{x \to \infty}(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x})\).
  • Aim: Evaluate the limit as \(x\) approaches infinity.

Core Concepts:

Indeterminate Forms: Direct substitution of \(\infty\) yields the indeterminate form \(\infty - \infty\).

Rationalization: For algebraic limits involving square roots and \(\infty - \infty\) forms, multiply and divide by the conjugate \((x + \sqrt{x^2+x})\) to convert to a manageable form, then simplify.

Solution:

  1. Rationalize the expression by multiplying by the conjugate:
    \[L = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{(x - \sqrt{x^2+x})(x + \sqrt{x^2+x})}{x + \sqrt{x^2+x}} \]
  2. Apply difference of squares \((a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2\):
    \[L = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{x^2 - (x^2 + x)}{x + \sqrt{x^2+x}} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)}} \]
  3. Simplify — since \(x \to \infty\), \(x\) is positive so \(\sqrt{x^2} = x\):
    \[L = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{-x}{x + x\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{x}}} \]
  4. Divide numerator and denominator by \(x\):
    \[L = \lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{x}}} \]
  5. Evaluate as \(x \to \infty\) (noting \(\dfrac{1}{x} \to 0\)):
    \[L = \dfrac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1+0}} = \dfrac{-1}{1+1} = -0.5 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: −0.5 | Option: B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: In the rigid-jointed frame shown in the figure, the distribution factor of the member AD is closest to
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Moment Distribution Method / Distribution Factor

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A rigid frame with central node A and four members:
    • AB: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(EI\), far end B is hinged.
    • AC: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(2EI\), far end C is free.
    • AF: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(2EI\), far end F is fixed.
    • AD: Non-prismatic — first half (\(L/2\)) has rigidity \(2EI\); second half (\(L/2\)) has rigidity \(EI\). Far end D is fixed.
  • Aim: Find the Distribution Factor (DF) for member AD at joint A.

Core Concepts:

Distribution Factor: \(DF_{AD} = \dfrac{K_{AD}}{\sum K}\), where \(K\) is the rotational stiffness at the joint.

Standard Rotational Stiffnesses:

  • Far end fixed: \(K = \dfrac{4EI}{L}\)
  • Far end hinged/pinned: \(K = \dfrac{3EI}{L}\)
  • Free end (cantilever): \(K = 0\)

Non-prismatic Member Stiffness: Derived using the Column Analogy Method, where the analogous column width = \(\dfrac{1}{EI_{actual}}\).

Solution:

  1. Stiffness of standard members:
    \(K_{AB} = \dfrac{3EI}{L}\) (far end pinned)
    \(K_{AC} = 0\) (far end free)
    \(K_{AF} = \dfrac{4(2EI)}{L} = \dfrac{8EI}{L}\) (far end fixed)
  2. Stiffness of member AD (Column Analogy):
    Segment 1 (near A): Width \(= \dfrac{1}{2EI}\), Length \(= L/2\) → Area \(A_1 = \dfrac{L}{4EI}\)
    Segment 2 (near D): Width \(= \dfrac{1}{EI}\), Length \(= L/2\) → Area \(A_2 = \dfrac{L}{2EI}\)
    Total Area: \(A = \dfrac{3L}{4EI}\)
  3. Centroid \(\bar{x}\) from A:
    \[\bar{x} = \dfrac{\dfrac{L}{4EI} \cdot \dfrac{L}{4} + \dfrac{L}{2EI} \cdot \dfrac{3L}{4}}{\dfrac{3L}{4EI}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{7L^2}{16EI}}{\dfrac{3L}{4EI}} = \dfrac{7L}{12} \]
  4. Moment of Inertia \(I_{xx}\) about centroid:
    \[I_1 = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2EI}(L/2)^3}{12} + \dfrac{L}{4EI}\left(\dfrac{7L}{12} - \dfrac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{19L^3}{576EI} \]
    \[I_2 = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{EI}(L/2)^3}{12} + \dfrac{L}{2EI}\left(\dfrac{3L}{4} - \dfrac{7L}{12}\right)^2 = \dfrac{14L^3}{576EI} \]
    \[I_{xx} = I_1 + I_2 = \dfrac{33L^3}{576EI} = \dfrac{11L^3}{192EI} \]
  5. Stiffness \(K_{AD}\) (stress at A for unit load \(P=1\) at A, eccentricity \(e = \dfrac{7L}{12}\)):
    \[K_{AD} = \dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{P \cdot e^2}{I_{xx}} = \dfrac{4EI}{3L} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7L}{12}\right)^2}{\dfrac{11L^3}{192EI}} = \dfrac{4EI}{3L} + \dfrac{196EI}{33L} = \dfrac{240EI}{33L} = \dfrac{80EI}{11L} \approx 7.273\dfrac{EI}{L} \]
  6. Total Joint Stiffness:
    \[\sum K = \dfrac{3EI}{L} + 0 + \dfrac{8EI}{L} + \dfrac{80EI}{11L} = \dfrac{11EI}{L} + \dfrac{80EI}{11L} = \dfrac{201EI}{11L} \approx 18.273\dfrac{EI}{L} \]
  7. Distribution Factor for AD:
    \[DF_{AD} = \dfrac{7.273}{18.273} = 0.398 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.398 | Option: C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q38

questions.question: In an oedometer apparatus a specimen of fully saturated clay has been consolidated under a vertical pressure of 100 kPa and is at equilibrium state. Immediately on increasing the vertical pressure to 150 kPa, the effective stress σ' and excess pore water pressure Δu will be
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Consolidation of Soils

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    Initial vertical pressure (equilibrium): \(\sigma_1 = 100\) kPa
    Vertical pressure immediately increased to: \(\sigma_2 = 150\) kPa
    Soil: Fully saturated clay.
  • Aim: Determine effective stress \(\sigma'\) and excess pore water pressure \(\Delta u\) immediately after the load increase.

Core Concepts:

Terzaghi's Principle of Effective Stress:

\[\sigma = \sigma' + u \]

Spring Analogy at \(t = 0\): Water is practically incompressible compared to the soil skeleton. In a fully saturated soil, immediately after an additional load \(\Delta\sigma\) is applied, water cannot drain instantaneously due to low permeability. Therefore, the entire load increment is initially carried by pore water: \(\Delta u = \Delta\sigma\). Effective stress does not change at \(t = 0\).

Solution:

  1. Initial Equilibrium State:
    Total stress \(\sigma_1 = 100\) kPa
    At equilibrium, excess pore pressure = 0
    ∴ Initial effective stress \(\sigma_1' = 100\) kPa
  2. Stress Increment:
    New total stress \(\sigma_2 = 150\) kPa
    Increment \(\Delta\sigma = 150 - 100 = 50\) kPa
  3. State Immediately After Loading (\(t = 0\)):
    Entire increment taken by pore water: \(\Delta u = \Delta\sigma = 50\) kPa
    Effective stress remains unchanged: \(\sigma' = \sigma_1' = 100\) kPa

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\sigma' = 100\) kPa, \(\Delta u = 50\) kPa | Option: B

questions.question: The speed-density relation on a one-way, single lane road is shown in the figure, where speed u is in km/hour and density k is in vehicles/km. The maximum flow (in vehicles/hour) on this road is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Speed-density (\(u\) vs \(k\)) relationship for a single-lane road:
    From \(k = 0\) to \(k = 10\): \(u\) is constant at 90 km/hr
    From \(k = 10\) to \(k = 100\): \(u\) drops linearly to 0
  • Aim: Determine the maximum flow \(q_{max}\) in vehicles/hour.

Core Concepts:

Fundamental Traffic Equation: Flow \((q)\) = Density \((k)\) × Speed \((u)\)

Optimization: Maximum flow occurs where \(\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0\).

Solution:

  1. Region 1 (\(0 \le k \le 10\)): Speed is constant at \(u = 90\) km/hr.
    \(q = k \times 90 = 90k\)
    Max flow at boundary \(k = 10\): \(q_{max1} = 90 \times 10 = 900\) veh/hr.
  2. Region 2 (\(10 \le k \le 100\)): Find linear equation through points (10, 90) and (100, 0).
    Slope \(m = \dfrac{0-90}{100-10} = -1\)
    Equation: \(u = 100 - k\)
  3. Maximize flow in Region 2:
    \[q = k(100-k) = 100k - k^2 \]
    \[\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 100 - 2k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 50 \text{ veh/km} \]
    \(k = 50\) is valid (within \([10, 100]\)).
    \[q_{max2} = 100(50) - (50)^2 = 5000 - 2500 = 2500 \text{ veh/hr} \]
  4. Compare: The absolute maximum flow is \(\max(900, 2500) = 2500\) veh/hr.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2500 veh/hr | Option: A

Structural Analysis | Shear Force & Bending Moment Diagrams

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Beam ACDEB — fixed at A, internal hinge at C, roller at E.
    Point load of 3 kN (↓) at C; Couple at D = 4 kN forces offset by 1 m above and below axis (forming a pure moment); Point load of 2 kN (↓) at B.
    Spans: AC = 5 m, CD = 2 m, DE = 2 m, EB = 2 m.
  • Aim: Identify correct statements regarding SF and BM distributions.

Core Concepts:

  • An internal hinge transmits shear force but cannot transmit bending moment (\(M = 0\) at hinge).
  • For compound beams, break at the internal hinge and solve the supported segment first, then transfer reactions.
  • A concentrated couple causes a sudden jump in BM but does not affect SF.

Solution:

  1. Resolve Couple at D:
    \[M_D = 4 \times 1 + 4 \times 1 = 8 \text{ kNm (clockwise)} \]
  2. Analyze Right Segment CEB (free body):
    Let \(V_{cR}\) = vertical reaction at hinge C (assume upward). Take moments about roller E (C is 4 m left of E):
    \[\sum M_E = 0: \quad V_{cR} \times 4 + 8 + 2 \times 2 = 0 \]
    \[4V_{cR} = -12 \Rightarrow V_{cR} = -3 \text{ kN} \]
    The left segment pulls the right segment downward with 3 kN.
  3. Analyze Left Segment AC (cantilever):
    By Newton's 3rd Law, right segment pushes left segment upward with 3 kN at C.
    External load at C = 3 kN (↓); reaction from hinge = 3 kN (↑).
    Net force at tip of AC = 0 kN → SF and BM are zero throughout AC. ✓ Statement (A) is True.
  4. Evaluate diagram jumps:
    At D: couple causes a jump in BM, not SF → Statement (B) is False.
    At E: roller reaction causes a jump in SF, not BM → Statement (C) is False.
  5. BM between D and E:

    BM at E (looking right): \(M_E = -(2 \times 2) = -4\) kNm
    BM changes from +2 to −4 kNm, so it passes through zero between D and E. ✓ Statement (D) is True.

Final Answer:

Total Hardness (TH): Caused by multivalent cations (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺), expressed as equivalent CaCO₃.

    \(MW_{MgCl_2} = 24 + (2 \times 35.5) = 95\) g/mol

    \[41x = 4180 \Rightarrow x \approx 101.95 \text{ mg} \]

  • Given Data: A facultative pond system used for wastewater treatment.

Core Concepts:

Algal-Bacterial Symbiosis: Facultative ponds rely on algae producing oxygen (photosynthesis) and bacteria consuming it to break down waste (respiration).

  • Daytime: Algae consume CO₂ and release O₂ via photosynthesis.
  • Nighttime: Without sunlight, photosynthesis stops. Both algae and bacteria respire, consuming O₂ and releasing CO₂.

Carbonate Buffer System: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), lowering pH. Removing CO₂ raises pH.

Solution:

  2. pH: During the day, algae strip CO₂ from water for photosynthesis — less CO₂ means less carbonic acid → higher (more alkaline) pH. At night, respiration pumps CO₂ back into water → lower pH. → pH is high during daytime compared to night-time. Statement (B) is True.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Statements A and B are true | Option(s): A; B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Let y be the solution of the initial value problem \( y'' + 0.8y' + 0.16y = 0 \), where \( y(0) = 3 \) and \( y'(0) = 4.5 \). Then, \( y(1) \) is equal to _______________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ODE: \(y'' + 0.8y' + 0.16y = 0\)
    Initial conditions: \(y(0) = 3\), \(y'(0) = 4.5\)
  • Aim: Evaluate \(y(1)\) rounded to 1 decimal place.

Core Concepts:

Second-order linear homogeneous ODE with constant coefficients. The nature of the roots of the characteristic equation determines the form of the general solution.

Solution:

  1. Characteristic Equation:
    \[r^2 + 0.8r + 0.16 = 0 \Rightarrow (r+0.4)^2 = 0 \]
    Roots are real and repeated: \(r = -0.4\).
  2. General Solution (repeated roots):
    \[y(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t)e^{-0.4t} \]
  3. Apply \(y(0) = 3\):
    \[3 = C_1 e^0 \Rightarrow C_1 = 3 \]
  4. Differentiate using product rule:
    \[y'(t) = C_2 e^{-0.4t} - 0.4(C_1 + C_2 t)e^{-0.4t} \]
  5. Apply \(y'(0) = 4.5\):
    \[4.5 = C_2 - 0.4(3) \Rightarrow C_2 = 4.5 + 1.2 = 5.7 \]
  6. Evaluate \(y(1)\):
    \[y(t) = (3 + 5.7t)e^{-0.4t} \]
    \[y(1) = (3 + 5.7) \times e^{-0.4} = 8.7 \times 0.67032 \approx 5.8317 \]
    Rounded to 1 decimal place: 5.8

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5.8 | NAT Key Range: 5.7 to 5.9

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q48

questions.question: The maximum value of the function \( h(x) = -x^3 + 2x^2 \) in the interval [-1,1.5] is equal to _______________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus / Maxima & Minima

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: \(h(x) = -x^3 + 2x^2\) on the closed interval \([-1,\ 1.5]\).
  • Aim: Find the maximum value of the function in the given interval, rounded to 1 decimal place.

Core Concepts:

Extreme Value Theorem: The absolute maximum of a continuous function on a closed interval occurs either at a critical point (where \(h'(x) = 0\)) or at one of the interval endpoints.

Solution:

  1. First Derivative:
    \[h'(x) = -3x^2 + 4x \]
  2. Critical Points (set \(h'(x) = 0\)):
    \[-x(3x-4) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ and } x = \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.333 \]
    Both lie within \([-1,\ 1.5]\).
  3. Evaluate \(h(x)\) at critical points and boundaries:
    \(x\)\(h(x)\)
    \(-1\) (boundary)\(-(-1)^3 + 2(-1)^2 = 1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}\)
    \(0\) (critical)\(0\)
    \(4/3\) (critical)\(-\dfrac{64}{27} + \dfrac{96}{27} = \dfrac{32}{27} \approx 1.185\)
    \(1.5\) (boundary)\(-3.375 + 4.5 = 1.125\)
  4. Global Maximum: Comparing all values (3, 0, 1.185, 1.125), the maximum occurs at \(x = -1\) with \(h(-1) = 3.0\).

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.0 | NAT Key Range: 2.9 to 3.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Consider the differential equation given below. Using the Euler method with the step size (h) of 0.5, the value of y at x = 1.0 is equal to _______________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).

\( \dfrac{dy}{dx} = y + 2x - x^2; \quad y(0) = 1 \quad (0 \le x < \infty) \)
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations / Euler Method

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    ODE: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y + 2x - x^2\)
    Initial condition: \(y(0) = 1\)
    Step size: \(h = 0.5\)
  • Aim: Find \(y\) at \(x = 1.0\) using the Euler method, rounded to 1 decimal place.

Core Concepts:

The Euler method is a first-order numerical procedure for solving ODEs with a given initial value.

\[y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot f(x_n, y_n) \]

Solution:

  1. Initialization: \(x_0 = 0\), \(y_0 = 1\), \(f(x,y) = y + 2x - x^2\)
  2. Step 1 — Find \(y_1\) at \(x_1 = 0.5\):
    Evaluate slope: \(f(0,1) = 1 + 2(0) - (0)^2 = 1\)
    \[y_1 = 1 + 0.5 \times 1 = 1.5 \]
  3. Step 2 — Find \(y_2\) at \(x_2 = 1.0\):
    Evaluate slope at \((0.5,\ 1.5)\):
    \[f(0.5,\ 1.5) = 1.5 + 2(0.5) - (0.5)^2 = 1.5 + 1.0 - 0.25 = 2.25 \]
    \[y_2 = 1.5 + 0.5 \times 2.25 = 1.5 + 1.125 = 2.625 \]
  4. Rounded to 1 decimal place: 2.6

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.6 | Range: 2.4 to 2.8

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: For the beam and loading shown in the figure, the second derivative of the deflection curve of the beam at the mid-point of AC is given by \( \alpha M_o / 8EI \). The value of \( \alpha \) is _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Beams / Euler-Bernoulli Bending

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Simply supported beam of total length \(2L\) with concentrated moment \(M_0\) at support A. Flexural rigidity: \(2EI\) for section AC (length \(L\)); \(EI\) for section CB (length \(L\)).
  • Aim: Find the coefficient \(\alpha\) where the second derivative of the deflection curve at the mid-point of AC equals \(\alpha M_0 / 8EI\).

Core Concepts:

The Euler-Bernoulli bending equation relates curvature to bending moment:

\[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{M}{EI_{local}} \]

To find the required value, we first determine support reactions and then the internal bending moment at the specified location.

Solution:

  1. Support Reactions (moment \(M_0\) applied clockwise at pin A):
    Taking moments about B:
    \[\sum M_B = 0 \implies R_A(2L) - M_0 = 0 \implies R_A = \dfrac{M_0}{2L} \text{ (downward)} \]
  2. Bending Moment at mid-point of AC (\(x = L/2\) from A):
    \[M_x = M_0 - R_A \cdot x = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0 x}{2L} \]
    \[M_{mid-AC} = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0 (L/2)}{2L} = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0}{4} = \dfrac{3M_0}{4} \]
  3. Curvature at mid-point of AC (local rigidity = \(2EI\)):
    \[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{3M_0/4}{2EI} = \dfrac{3M_0}{8EI} \]
  4. Extract \(\alpha\):
    Comparing \(\dfrac{3M_0}{8EI}\) with \(\alpha \dfrac{M_0}{8EI}\): \(\alpha = 3\)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\alpha = \) 3 | Range: 3 to 3
